claims.text: Steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications resist corrosion because they form a stable, alloy-enriched passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film limits diffusion of corrosive species into the underlying metal.
The passive oxide film is enriched in chromium and nickel.
Corrosion-resistant alloying elements promote selective oxidation at the steel surface.
Selective oxidation creates a passive film with low diffusivity for corrosive agents.
The low-diffusivity passive film acts as a barrier that significantly slows corrosion under harsh operating conditions.
Steels with higher chromium and nickel levels will form thicker passive oxide films than lower-alloy steels under identical conditions.
Steels with higher chromium and nickel levels will form more adherent passive oxide films than lower-alloy steels under identical conditions.
Thicker and more adherent passive films will result in significantly lower corrosion rates than those of lower-alloy baseline steels.
Lower levels of corrosion-resistant alloying elements lead to minimal continuous oxide-film formation.
The proposed passive-film mechanism holds within the temperature, radiation, and chemical-aggressiveness regimes representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Conditions outside the stated operational regimes may activate alternative corrosion processes.
Comparable films and corrosion rates in low- and high-alloy steels under identical conditions would falsify the proposed alloy-enriched-film mediation mechanism.
